messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

I would like to fit the following model

$$ y_(ij) ~ N(\mu_j,\sigma^2_j)   (1) $$

where i denote individual and j group.

Here is a simulation

n.group <- 8
n.rep <- 100
group <- gl(n.group,n.rep)
mu <- rnorm(n.group)
sigmasq <- n.rep*runif(n.group)
y <- rnorm(length(group),mean=mu[group],sd=sqrt(sigmasq[group]))

And I used a latent field for each group to model the likelihood

X <- model.matrix(y~group+0)
idx <- matrix(1:nrow(X),nrow(X),ncol(X))
colnames(idx) <- paste("i",1:ncol(X),sep=".")
f.group <- paste("f(",colnames(idx),",",colnames(X),",model='iid')",sep="")
formula <- as.formula(paste("y ~ group+",paste(f.group,collapse="+"),sep=""))
formula
require(INLA)
fit <- inla(formula,family="gaussian",data=as.data.frame(cbind(y,X,idx)),
            control.family=list(hyper=list(theta=list(initial=10,fixed=TRUE))))

The output appears consistent.

plot(mu,fit$summary.fixed$mean,xlab="mu",ylab="fit",main="average")
plot(1/sigmasq,fit$summary.hyper[,4],xlab="prec",ylab="fit",main="precision")

But this will not accommodate group-specific t likelihood, I know it is possible to define separate likelihood for each group, but it seems error prone for more groups, and complex if I use a mean structure with other spatial or temporal random effects.

Is there an easier way to implement this model (1) in INLA? If so, can it be generalized to t likelihood?

Regards
dong

> Such nonlinear transformations are easiest to handle by transforming samples generated by
> inla.posterior.sample()
>
> Finn
>
> Finn
>
> On 29 Sep 2015, at 13:59, Erick Okuto <erick...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Dear Elias and Finn,
> > With your help, I have been able to fit a dynamic model as outlined above.
> >
> > Two dynamic covariates (cos and sin amplitudes) have been used. The number of hyperparameters were 10 when a random intercept is added hence the need for a non-random intercept for computational reasons, unless there is a trick! The R-code and test data  used is shared below.
> >
> > My major concern now is how we can extract (assuming they have been computed) the spatially varying regression coefficients (b1 and b2) for each pixel/coordinate. I need the coefficients at pixel level which can be helpful.
> >
> > For example:
> > Model1
> > f(t) =  b1*cos(w*t) + b2*sin (w*t)  with b1 and b2 being cos and sine amplitudes (this can be computed with R-INLA)
> >
> > which can be expressed in polar coordinates as in model2
> >
> > Model2
> > f(t) = B* cos(w*t + phi) where w=constant (2*pi/k) and k is the time dimension (May be, could be against LGM requirements in INLA)
> >
> > #But, there is a relationship between model1 and model2
> > i.e  B=sqrt(b1^2 + b2^2) = which denote annual amplitude and in phenology, this parameter is useful in providing information on season timings (e.g start and end of growing season).
> >
> > Also, phi=tan^-1(-[b1/b2]) i.e. tan(phi)=- b1/b2 which we can obtain from model1. This parameter is the annual phase which provides some information about green-up/peak.
> >
> > Therefore, the two parameters (annual amplitude and phase) are the major stories which should be obtained at pixel/coordinate level
> >
> > Any help and/or suggestion will be appreciated.
> >
> > Thanks in advance.
> >
> >
> > # The R-code
> >
> > require(INLA)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #  Test record from Tranzoia county in Kenya
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > tranzoiadata=read.csv("F:/CLIM_DATA/tranzoia_county/combine.tranz.csv")
> > tranzoiadata2=tranzoiadata[, 1:14]
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #   defining the spatial locations
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > n <- nrow(tranzoiadata2[, -c(1:2)])
> > k <- ncol(tranzoiadata2[,-c(1:2)])
> >
> > coo <- as.matrix(tranzoiadata2[1:n, 1:2])
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #We sample from a random field on a set of location:
> > #We use the above function to draw k (number of time points)
> > #samples from the random field
> > #####################################################
> > rrf <- function(n, coords, kappa, variance, nu=1) {
> >   m <- as.matrix(dist(coords))
> >   m <- exp((1-nu)*log(2) + nu*log(kappa*m)-lgamma(nu))*besselK(m*kappa, nu)
> >   diag(m) <- 1
> >   chol(variance*m)%*%matrix(rnorm(nrow(coords)*n), ncol=n)
> > }
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #we make it temporally correlated considering an autoregression of order 1:
> > #where the 1-rho[2]^2 term is in accord to the parametrization
> > #of the AR(1) model in INLA
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > kappa <- c(8, 8); sigma2 <- c(1/3, 1/3)
> > rho <- c(0.8, 0.8)
> > beta1 <- rrf(k, coo, kappa[1], sigma2[1]) * (1-rho[1]^2)
> > beta2 <- rrf(k, coo, kappa[2], sigma2[2]) * (1-rho[2]^2)
> >
> > for (j in 2:k) {
> >   beta1[, j] <- beta1[,j-1]*rho[1] + beta1[,j]
> >   beta2[, j] <- beta2[,j-1]*rho[2] + beta2[,j]
> > }
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #creating the regression covariates cos and sine amplitude terms
> > #The two are necessary to compute annual phase and growing season length
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > w=2*pi/k
> > time.mat=round(matrix(rep(w*(1:k/k), each=n), nrow=n), 4)
> > cos.amplitude <- round(matrix(cos(time.mat),  nrow=n), 4) ### covariate1
> > sine.amplitude <- round(matrix(sin(time.mat), nrow=n), 4) ### covariate2
> >
> > tranzoiadata3=round(as.matrix(tranzoiadata2[, -(1:2)]), 4)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #To get the response, we do simulations for the covariate,
> > #compute the mean and add an error term
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> >
> > taue <- 5
> >
> > y <- as.vector(tranzoiadata3)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #Fitting the model as sugested in the SPDE tutorial :
> > #y = B0 + x1(Aξ1) + x2(Aξ2) + e
> > #To work out the second  and third term in the right side of the last
> > #equation we just need to supply the covariate values as the
> > #weights argument in the inla.spde.make.A() function
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > (mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(coo, max.edge=0.25, offset=0.05, cutoff=0.05))$n
> > (spde <- inla.spde2.matern(mesh))$n.spde
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > # projector matrices and the indexes set as follows
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > A1 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, cbind(rep(coo[,1], k), rep(coo[,2], k)),
> >                        group=rep(1:k, each=n), weights=as.vector(cos.amplitude))
> > A2 <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, cbind(rep(coo[,1], k), rep(coo[,2], k)),
> >                        group=rep(1:k, each=n), weights=as.vector(sine.amplitude))
> >
> > i1 <- inla.spde.make.index('i1', spde$n.spde, n.group=k)
> > i2 <- inla.spde.make.index('i2', spde$n.spde, n.group=k)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > # The data stack is as follows
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > stk.y <- inla.stack(data=list(y=y), tag='y',
> >                     A=list(A1, A2, 1),
> >                     effects=list(i1, i2,
> >                     data.frame(mu1=1, cos.amplitude=as.vector(cos.amplitude),
> >                     sine.amplitude=as.vector(sine.amplitude))))
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #A non-random (for computational reasons) intercept (mu1)
> > #is added
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > formula <- y ~ 0 + mu1 + cos.amplitude + sine.amplitude +
> >   f(i1, model=spde, group=i1.group, control.group=list(model='ar1')) +
> >   f(i2, model=spde, group=i2.group, control.group=list(model='ar1'))
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #we define starting values for the hyperparameters in the
> > #internal scale considering the values used to simute the data
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > (theta.ini <- c(log(taue),
> >                 -log(4*pi*sigma2[1]*kappa[1]^2)/2, log(kappa[1]),
> >                 log((1+rho[1])/(1-rho[1])),
> >                 -log(4*pi*sigma2[2]*kappa[2]^2)/2, log(kappa[2]),
> >                 log((1+rho[2])/(1-rho[2]))))
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #   Fitting the model considering the initial values defined above
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > res <- inla(formula, family='gaussian', data=inla.stack.data(stk.y),
> >             control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.y), compute = FALSE),
> >             control.mode=list(theta=theta.ini, restart=TRUE),
> >             verbose=FALSE)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #Extracting the spataily dependent regression parameters
> > #for each pixel/coordinate
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> >
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #Fixed effects (annual mean, cos and sine amplitude) estimates
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > round(cbind(res$summary.fix), 4)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #Summary of the posterior marginal density for the AR1 process
> > #for each of the random fields
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > round(cbind(res$summary.hy[c(4, 7), ]), 4)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #   The results for the two random fields
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > rf1 <- inla.spde2.result(res, 'i1', spde, do.transf=TRUE)
> > rf2 <- inla.spde2.result(res, 'i2', spde, do.transf=TRUE)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #The practical range of the spatio-temporal process
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > round(cbind(prior=sqrt(8)/kappa, t(sapply(list(rf1, rf2),
> >              function(rrf) unlist(inla.zmarginal(
> >              rrf$marginals.range.nom[[1]], silent=TRUE))))), 3)
> >
> > #Variance for each spatio-temporal process
> > round(cbind(prior=sigma2, t(sapply(list(rf1, rf2), function(rrf)
> >   unlist(inla.zmarginal(rrf$marginals.variance.nominal[[1]],
> >                         silent=TRUE))))), 3)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > #   Scaling/smoothing parameter estimate
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > round(cbind(prior=kappa, t(sapply(list(rf1, rf2), function(rrf)
> >   unlist(inla.zmarginal(rrf$marginals.kappa[[1]], silent=TRUE))))), 3)
> >
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>
> > # Using cos and sine amplitude estimates to estimate annual phase
> > # and growing season length
> > #>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

I want to a spatial dataset. The data set is of form (x,y;z), where (x,y) are the coordinates, and z is the associated observation at that location.

This should be a quite common assumption in geology that some uncertainty depend on the values themselves. I don't know whether/how can INLA implement such modeling? Thanks in advance!

Best regards,

On Thu, 2015-10-08 at 08:09 -0700, David Wang wrote:
> Dear INLA community,

> I want to a spatial dataset. The data set is of form (x,y;z), where
> (x,y) are the coordinates, and z is the associated observation at
> that location.
> Basically, suppose there ia a true surface (x,y;z0), then the
> error/uncertainty in the observation z can be roughly divided into
> two parts: a, which is independent of (x,y;z0) and b, which is
> depending on z0 saying e.g. 2% of z0.

What you're asking for is a combination of additive and multiplicative
errors, e.g.
  z(x,y) = z0(x,y) * (1 + e2(x,y)) + e1(x,y)

Each type by itself is fine (multiplicative errors become additive in
log scale), but the combination is tricky.  If the errors are small
relative to the magnitude of the true surface, the approximation
  z(x,y) = z0(x,y) + z(x,y) * e2(x,y) + e1(x,y)
can be used:
  formula <-
    z ~ model_components_for_z0_go_here + f(e2, z, model="iid")
This sets up "z" to be used as weights for iid normal random
variables, as in the formula above.
The additive errors will come from the the data likelihood model:
  inla(formula, data=data, family="normal")

For certain types of surface models there are tricks that allow a
better approximation of multiplicative errors, but as indicated by the
word, the are more tricky to use.

Finn

Hi,

the main issue is that the double laplace has zero second deriviate of
the log likelihood, although there is an overall 'curvature'. this
means that there is no local information in the likelihood about the
variance, just the mean. there are also problems with the numerical
optimizer in this case.

I doubt that laplace approximations are adequate for this case, and
something else must be done. OR, there is some empirical evidence that
the estimates achived are good (mean and especially the variance).

For these reasons, it is disabled.

It is possible to do parametric quantile regression instead, of
course...

Hi!

For the modelling, have a look at chapter 6 of Banerjee Carlin &
Gelfand (2004) Hierarchical Modeling and Analysis for Spatial Data. If
I understand your problem, you have 2 maps which each partition the
region - one administrative and one from Corine - incidence data for
one and the other is a covariate in the model.

The BCG approach is to make a new partition by overlaying the two maps
to create a new one simply by merging the lines. Each administrative
polygon is then made up of several land use polygons ("atoms"). If the
expected disease incidence in each atom is lambda, then the incidence
in the administrative region is the sum of the lambdas, and the number
of cases follows a Poisson distribution with mean equal to this sum.

I had a slightly similar problem last year, and I don't think INLA can
deal this, because your likelihood is of the form

X ~ Po(sum \lambda) = Po(sum exp(sum \beta X))

which will look horrible.

I don't know if you could do some imputation. Given a count N in an
administrative region, the number of cases in each atom is
multinomial, so you might be able to use that to simulate the cases in
each atom, fit the model, and then average (somehow) over the imputed
data.

Hopefully there's a better solution to this...

Bob

Hi everyone,

I have ran into an issue when trying to run a coregionalization model based on two LGCPs,

The script initially ran fine on my laptop (with just an i5 dualcore 2.4 Ghz processor and 4 Gb of ram (windows 7). It reached 100% utilisation and finished just fine.

For the final results I transferred it to my (more powerful) desktop to change the settings for the final result.
Settings I have changed:
-Changed time knots from 6 to 23 (representing a 69 day time period).
-Changed settings for finer spatial mesh (from 235) to 948 nodes
-Removed argument:  control.inla=list(strategy='gaussian')), leaving the call to inla (for the first LGCP) as:

Incidents.res <- inla(form_I, family='poisson',
                      data=inla.stack.data(stk_I), E=expect,
                      control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk_I)))

When running the script the first LGCP ran for over 16 hours before I stopped it (as the complete model would just take too long at this rate (mind you that this first LGCP only has an n of 230 (the second has an n of 2489))).

Monitoring the CPU utilization showed this:
-Total CPU usage never exceeded 64%, mainly staying around 40%, but also sitting at around 10-20% for prolonged periods of time.
-All of the 8 threads were being used, with all of them showing short spikes to 100% seperately.
-RAM usage seemed to sit at around 5 Gb (of 16) (although this was a snapshot (I did not monitor it constantly).

I find it strange that the total CPU utilization almost never gets above 50 %. I have come across the num.threads argument, but since all threads are used this does not seem likely to resolve the problem (also I've tried num.threads=8 and num.threads=4 shortly (stopping the run after a few minutes after I did not notice increased utilization). Perhaps I am wrong of course.

Now my question is if there is a way to shorten the computational time (apart from lowering the time knots and spatial nodes), such as increasing CPU utilization?

To emphasize; the script ran fine (with the cruder settings), it just takes very long when using the above settings (disproportionately long I think).

System information:
CPU: i7-4790k (quadcore 4.4 Ghz, with 8 threads (HT))
Ram: 16 Gb ddr3
OS: Windows 8.1 64bit
R-version: Fire safety 3.2.2 64 bit

I very much hope that someone here knows of a solution for this and that I have adequately explained the issue.

Thanks,
Marco Stam

  With control.fixed = list(expand.factor.strategy='model.matrix'), then NA's in factor are not allowd. Please use strategy 'inla' instead.

My question is this: why does this error occur when there are no NA values in my data? Is this just because some mesh vertices are at unobserved points?

Error in `contrasts<-`(`*tmp*`, value = contr.funs[1 + isOF[nn]]) :
  contrasts can be applied only to factors with 2 or more levels

Is there a recommended approach for dealing with this problem(s) aside from using 0/1 dummy variables to get around it, or something obvious that I am overlooking? Thanks for your time.

-tyler scott

The issue is that factors and NA doesn't always play nicely, in particular in combination with inla.stack, which has as one of its purposes to add NA:s where needed to construct certain linear combination predictors. The "inla" expansion strategy should be stable in that situation, but the default one isn't.  Factors are _always_ expanded as 0/1 dummy variables internally, it's just that in this case it needs more specific guidance about exactly how to do that expansion.

I'm not sure why the second error occurs.

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am trying to do a spatial analysis using a basic geostatistical model: mean only (no covariates) and the Matern latent Gaussian field.  The R-INLA estimation process gives me sensible results and is quick about it too.  So, all is good in terms of estimation.

My problem comes in trying to summarise the results for subsequent analyses.  In particular, I would like to be able to generate samples from the joint posterior of the mean and the hyperparameters.  It would be great to generate them from the joint distribution.  I have been trying with the inla.posterior.sample(), which superficially gives what I want -- but the simulated values for the hyperparameters are discretised (presumably to the points where the INLA approximation has occurred). I have also looked at inla.hyperparameter.sample(), but that does not sample from fixed effects.  Is there a hybrid function that I am missing?

Finally, just to confirm my understanding:  Is there any way to estimate / sample from the joint distribution of the latent field? I understand that this is an area that is still-to-be-resolved.

Any help appreciated.  Thanks in advance,

Nick
